title: Potiphar's house (Genesis 39)
hookLine: Joseph rises, is falsely accused, and lands in prison

cards: Joseph is up for sale again. Not long ago he was the favorite son with the fancy coat.

Since then he's been thrown in a pit by his own brothers, sold to strangers, carried down to Egypt, and sold again, far from everyone he knows. An Egyptian official named Potiphar, captain of Pharaoh's guard, buys him.
Joseph has every reason to shut down. To do the minimum. To be bitter for the rest of his life.

teach.b: The chapter opens with a line that becomes its drumbeat: "And the LORD was with Joseph, and he was a prosperous man." Joseph works, and everything he touches goes well.
Potiphar notices, and soon puts him in charge of the whole house. Then, trouble. Potiphar's wife wants Joseph, and asks him, day after day.

teach.h: HOW CAN I DO THIS GREAT WICKEDNESS?
teach.b: He refuses, and his answer is about loyalty and about God: his master trusted him with everything, so "how then can I do this great wickedness, and sin against God?"

teach.h: A GARMENT USED TO LIE, AGAIN.
teach.b: One day, when the house is empty, she grabs his garment. He runs, and leaves it in her hand. And she uses it.

She tells the household, then her husband, that the Hebrew slave attacked her, and holds up the garment as proof. Notice: this is the second time a piece of Joseph's clothing is used to tell a lie about him.
First the coat, dipped in blood. Now this.
So Joseph, who did the right thing, lands in prison. And here's the part that makes the chapter: the same line comes back. The LORD was with Joseph.
In prison. The keeper of the prison notices him, and soon Joseph is running the place, looking after the other prisoners.
Nothing in the story says the pit or the prison was good. What it says is that Joseph kept being Joseph wherever they put him. Honest in the good house.

how: Jewish tradition calls Joseph Yosef ha-Tzaddik, Joseph the righteous, and rabbinic teaching ties the title to how he acted in Potiphar's house.

games.q: you're Joseph, a slave now running your master's whole house. your master's wife keeps pressing you, day after day. what do you do?
games.why: he refuses: "how then can I do this great wickedness, and sin against God?" when she grabs his garment he runs, and she uses it to accuse him.

practice: Think of a place in your life that isn't good right now: a job you'd leave if you could, a tense home, a hospital room, a situation that isn't fair.
Then think of one small good thing you could still do there, like helping one person, doing one task well, or being honest when it's easier not to be. You don't have to pretend the place is fine.
